## Abstract

Aluminum (Al) alloys are pivotal structural materials, indispensable for advanced

energy-saving solutions and lightweight technologies. However, the limited heat

resistance and low critical strength of the present commercial Al alloys at elevated

temperatures (300-400 °C) have constrained their broader applications. Here, we present

a facile strategy to additively manufacture strong yet ductile heat-resistant Al alloys using

laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB). By embedding heat-resistant multicomponent

intermetallic nanophases (HMINPs) at the solidified cell boundaries, the as-printed alloy

forms thermally stable cellular structures containing a high-volume fraction (~14 vol%) of

HMINPs. Without any additional post-treatment, our as-printed Al alloy exhibits an

average room-temperature tensile strength of 582 MPa, combined with a tensile strength

of 114 MPa and exceptional creep resistance at 400 °C. The partial solid-state

amorphization of the HMINPs during tensile straining at 300–400 °C creates a nano-dual-

phase glass–crystal structure, providing an additional toughening mechanism. This

HMINP strategy and PBF-LB's freeform manufacturing capability enable large-scale

industrial use of our high-performance Al alloy, holding great promise for advancing

energy efficiency, carbon neutrality, and sustainable manufacturing.

## Introduction

Metal additive manufacturing (AM), or three-dimensional (3D) printing, has emerged

as an innovative net-shape forming technology that enables the rapid fabrication of

complex components directly from computer-aided design models, holding appeal for a


<!-- Page 5 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

diverse range of applications1-3. During AM, such as laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB),

the micro-scale melting pools (MPs), intrinsic steep temperature gradient (106–107 °C/m),

and rapid cooling rate coupled with the extreme thermal cycles give rise to distinctive, far-

from-equilibrium microstructures3,4. Among these, solidification-induced cellular

structures are a characteristic feature that is rarely attainable through conventional

casting or welding. Such cellular microstructures have now been reported across a wide

range of alloy systems produced via PBF-LB, including Ti alloys2, steels4,5, Al alloys6, Ni-

based superalloys7 and high-entropy alloys8. The cell walls or boundaries often exhibit

pronounced compositional segregation from the matrix, allowing the introduction of

precipitate skeleton architecture characterized by the secondary phases embedded in the

cell boundaries to enhance the mechanical performance5,6,9. This architectural design

accommodates substantial dislocation activity during deformation, offering a means to

tailor work hardening behavior and achieve high strength4,9.

Al alloys are the most common lightweight alloys, and have been widely used in

many critical fields due to their high specific strength and the abundance of natural

resources10-12. However, a significant drawback of these lightweight Al alloys is their low

heat resistance at elevated temperatures (300–400 °C), which limits their use in advanced

engineering applications that require high service temperatures13,14. Conventional high-

strength heat-resistant Al alloys, such as cast A201 and wrought 2618 Al alloys, suffer

from issues such as rapid coarsening of strengthening precipitates driven by the

extensive thermal diffusion and insufficient volume fraction of these precipitates,


<!-- Page 6 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

ultimately reducing load-bearing capacity at elevated temperatures15. Although certain Al

alloys can incorporate precipitates with a large volume fraction, such as θ’-Al2Cu and η’-

MgZn2, these precipitates typically comprise solutes with high-solubility and fast-diffusion

rates, and therefore lack sufficient thermal stability15,16. In contrast, precipitates with high

thermal stability, such as Al3Sc and Al3Zr, are composed of slow-diffusing solutes, making

it difficult to achieve an adequate volume fraction for effective strengthening17,18.

Consequently, the dissimilarity in solute diffusivities hinders the formation of

nanoprecipitates with both high stability and a high volume fraction, which are crucial for

developing heat-resistant Al alloys. Recent advances highlight strategies for attaining

high-temperature strength in Al alloys by stabilizing networks of eutectic precipitates

during PBF-LB. Examples include thermally stable nanoscale Al-La eutectic cellular

networks19 and Cu/Mn-stabilized networks of Al₆Fe phase20. Furthermore, Ren et al.

enhanced thermal stability by dispersing spherical amorphous precipitates (~20 nm in

size) within the cell interiors and along cell boundaries21.

Here, we propose a facile and green strategy to develop advanced heat-resistant Al

alloy by importing a highly thermal stable cellular structure via PBF-LB (Fig. 1a). Our

approach is based on creating a controlled distribution of high-density, strong and heat-

resistant multicomponent intermetallic nanophases (HMINPs) at the cell boundaries,

which provides effective strengthening in Al alloys (Fig. 1b). By actively tailoring

precipitation behavior during PBF-LB, we utilize the major impurities in recycled Al alloys,

including high-solubility Si and slow-diffusing transition elements (Mn, Ni, Fe), to form a


<!-- Page 7 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

high-volume fraction of α-type Al(FeMnNi)Si HMINPs. This stabilizes the nanoprecipitates

through solute segregation and blocking reverse interface diffusion16,22. Combining the

thermal stability derived from the multicomponent complex nature23 with the additional

dislocation storage capacity offered by the heterogeneous cellular structures10, our

conceptual design extends thermal stability to higher service temperatures while

maintaining superior mechanical performance. Moreover, the limited addition of the

readily abundant Fe, Mn, Ni elements, together with a high Si content, helps preserve the

lightweight nature of the alloy. Thus, the present alloy design eschews expensive/rare-

earth elements (e.g., Sc, Ag, Ta) and requires no post-treatment, making it highly

promising for industrial-scale adoption.

## Results and Discussion

Thermally stable microstructures

We printed the heat-resistant Al alloys via PBF-LB using gas-atomized powders with

a chemical composition of Al-7.44Si-2.34Fe-1.79Mn-1.12Ni (wt %) (Supplementary Fig.

1a-d). Through careful optimization of the processing parameters, the as-printed samples

achieved near-full density with a relative density of up to 99.99%, demonstrating excellent

printability, as verified by the micro-focus computed tomography (micro-CT) results

(Supplementary Fig. 1e-f). Side-view cross-sectional analysis revealed a bi-modal grain

size distribution: columnar grains spanning the MPs alongside fine equiaxed grains

adjacent to the MP boundaries (Supplementary Fig. 2a). The average grain size was 12.5


<!-- Page 8 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

μm, with no significant crystallographic texture (Supplementary Fig. 2b-c). Representative

cellular structures in the as-printed condition are shown in Fig. 1c-d. Scanning electron

microscopy (SEM) images (Fig. 1c) displayed MPs consisting of fine cells measuring 300-

400 nm. The cell size transitioned from fine cells within the MPs to relatively coarser cells

near the MP boundaries, reflecting local variations in thermal history because of the

overlaps of adjacent MPs during the layer-by-layer deposition3,4. The transmission

electron microscopy-energy dispersive spectroscopy (TEM-EDS) mapping (Fig. 1d)

illustrated that the cellular structure forms a co-continuous framework of HMINP networks

and Al dendritic-cell, where interconnected Al cells are encircled by the HMINPs that

constitute the cell boundaries. The network skeleton width was approximately 60 nm, and

the volume fraction of HMINPs was estimated to be about 14 %. It is worth noting that the

cell boundaries were present both within the grain interior and between adjacent grains

(Supplementary Fig. 2d).

In addition to the HMINPs, Si nanoparticles were also observed, and some located

near the HMINPs (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig. 3a). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern

(Fig. 1e) indicated that the HMINPs possessed a crystal structure akin to the α-type

Al(M)Si phases (where M represents transition elements such as Mn, Fe, Cr, etc.)24.

Notably, these α-type phases, exemplified by the Al(Mn,Mo)Si phase25 in cast Al alloy and

α-Al(FeMn)Si phase26 in 3D-printed Al alloy, play a critical role in high-temperature

strengthening. We subsequently employed 3D atom probe tomography (APT) to further

analyze the typical elemental distribution of HMINPs within grain interiors and at grain

boundaries. As illustrated in Fig. 1f, noticeable elemental partitioning is evident between

the HMINPs at different locations and the Al matrix, with Si nanoparticles also detected

adjacent to the HMINPs. Despite minor composition undulations within the HMINPs, Al

and Si are significantly enriched, reaching average concentrations of approximately 60

at% and 20 at%, respectively. Enrichment of Fe (~10 at %), Mn (~5 at %), and Ni (~4 at %)

was also confirmed (Supplementary Fig. 3b-g and Supplementary Table 1). The atomic

structure of the present HMINPs was further resolved by the scanning TEM with

aberration corrector (AC-STEM) technique. As displayed in Fig. 1g, the high-angle

annular dark-field (HAADF) and corresponding fast Fourier transformation (FFT) patterns

revealed that a semi-coherent interface between the superlattice-structured HMINPs and

the Al matrix. Atomic-scale STEM images and EDS mapping along various zone axes

indicate that these HMINPs adopt a Pm3 cubic crystal structure with a lattice constant of

1.256 nm, wherein the transition elements are readily interchangeable (Supplementary

*Fig. 4a-e). Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) curves of the as-printed Al alloy*

suggest that these HMINPs form initially during solidification (Supplementary Fig. 4f-g),

leading us to identify them as the quinary α-Al(FeMnNi)Si phases.

We then performed in-situ TEM heating experiments (Supplementary Fig. 5a) to

directly visualize the microstructure evolution during short time heating process of our Al

alloy at various temperatures (200 °C, 300 °C and 400 °C). The microstructure remained

largely unchanging at temperatures below 300 °C, while there were subtle changes in the

Al grains at 400 °C. The coarsening behavior of the HMINPs was investigated by

subjecting bulk specimens (our alloy and AlSi10Mg for comparison) to thermal exposure

at 400 °C for durations of 1–168 hours. It is evident that after 168 hours of exposure, the

MP boundaries remain distinct and the HMINPs exhibit no significant coarsening or

dissolving (Supplementary Fig. 5b). In contrast, in the AlSi10Mg sample, the Si network

is disrupted, and the Si particles exhibit pronounced coarsening. This is significantly vital

as the rapid coarsening or dissolution of nanoprecipitates in Al alloys often eventuates

accelerated failures at elevated temperatures15-17. Therefore, the excellent heat

resistance of the cell structure formed by the continuous HMINPs in our Al alloy is

expected to promote the thermal stability of our heat-resistant Al alloys at high

temperatures.

Exceptional mechanical properties and commercial uses

To evaluate the mechanical performance of the newly developed Al alloy with highly

thermally stable microstructure, a comprehensive series of tensile and creep tests were

conducted across a range of temperatures (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Fig. 2a

presents the representative tensile engineering stress–strain curves for the as-printed

alloy tested in both transverse and longitudinal directions from 25 to 400 °C. Overall,


<!-- Page 12 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

tensile stress decreases while elongation increases with rising temperature. Remarkably,

our heat-resistant Al alloy effectively minimizes the pronounced mechanical anisotropy

typically seen in most Al alloys fabricated by PBF-LB. At 25 °C, it exhibits a yield strength

(σY) of ~440 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (σUTS) of ~582 MPa, and an elongation (EL)

of ~7.2% along both directions. This excellent strength-ductility balance is comparable to

that of the strongest wrought 7xxx series Al alloys and surpasses most Al alloys printed

by PBF-LB27-33. Even at elevated temperatures, where most Al alloys suffer from

premature failure due to limited heat resistance, our alloy retains high performance. For

example, it maintains a high σUTS of ~263 MPa at 300 °C and ~114 MPa even at 400 °C.

Compared with previously reported high-strength Al alloys fabricated by PBF-LB and

conventional routes, our as-printed Al alloy shows clearly superior mechanical properties

at both room and elevated temperatures (Fig. 2b) 14,16,27-37. Tensile creep tests performed

at 400 °C under stresses of 25-40 MPa to reveal the alloy’s strong resistance to time-

dependent deformation (Fig. 2c). In comparison with previously reported Al alloys16,38-41,

the heat-resistant Al alloy exhibited low steady-state creep rates, demonstrating superior

creep resistance (Fig. 2d). While certain alloys (e.g., cast Al–Cu–Mg–Ag–Sc16) may

achieve higher creep resistance, they often rely on costly elements such as Ag and Sc.

In contrast, the present alloy delivers robust performance over a wide temperature range

without requiring post heat treatment. This outcome not only reflects advances in AM

techniques but also underscores the distinct advantages of our strategy.

Deformation mechanisms

To elucidate the origins underlying the exceptional heat-resistant properties exhibited

in our alloy, we conducted an exhaustive analysis of the deformation microstructures

ranging from microscopic to atomic scales. We captured the microstructure near the

fracture region after creep rupture under 400 °C and 25 MPa tensile stress to analyze the

evolution of defects and HMINPs. Under such extreme conditions, the specimen achieved

a high creep life of approximately 330 hours. The MP boundaries near the fracture


<!-- Page 15 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

remained intact and clearly discernible, and the fracture was observed to propagate along

them, with the majority of creep-induced cavities located adjacent to them

(Supplementary Fig. 8a). Despite some evident coarsening under stress and long-term

thermal exposure, the HMINPs retained sizes ranging from tens to a few hundred

nanometers (Supplementary Fig. 8b-c), demonstrating robust thermal stability. Similarly,

the nanoprecipitate network also remained intact following tensile testing at 400 °C

(Supplementary Fig. 9a-b). Tensile deformation was primarily associated with typical

dislocation slips (Supplementary Fig. 9c-d) and the accumulation of dislocation around

the precipitates suggested a robust dislocation-precipitate interaction. Furthermore, post-

fracture analysis revealed a significant rise in kernel average misorientation values within

the tested specimen (Supplementary Fig. 9e-k), highlighting the efficacy of geometrically

necessary dislocations in accommodating deformation5.

Intriguingly, amorphization zones were identified near the crack tips in the samples

fractured during tensile testing at 400 °C (Fig. 3a). A similar phenomenon was observed

in specimens tested at 300 °C but was scarcely discernible at lower temperatures. Fig.

3b elucidates the coexistence of a large crystalline region, containing HMINPs and Si

particles, with an adjacent amorphous area. The interface between the amorphous zone

and Al matrix appears remarkably straight, as outlined by the dotted lines in Fig. 3b. This

distinct geometric relationship is further illustrated in Fig. 3c, a finding rarely reported in

the literature. Fig. 3d unveils rod-like and globular supra-nano-sized particles (smaller

than 5 nm) uniformly dispersed within the amorphous phase, thereby constituting a nano-


<!-- Page 16 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

dual-phase glass-crystal structure termed an “amorphous + supra-nano precipitate”

composite. HADDF-STEM analysis (Fig. 3e) validates that these precipitates in the

amorphous region correspond to L12-ordered γ’-(Ni,Fe)3Al phases, which are known for

enhancing toughness and thermal stability in Ni-based or Co-based superalloys42. This

nano-dual-phase glass-crystal architectural configuration, previously unreported in bulk

Al alloys, highlights the exceptional attributes of our material. APT examination of the

amorphous zone indicated a chemical composition in close congruence with that of the

HMINPs (Supplementary Fig. 10a-e), suggesting the amorphous region originated from

the partial transformation of HMINPs. Such amorphous phase transitions are often

reported in high-entropy systems due to the nature of the inherent atomic-scale

complexity and local chemical disorder in multicomponent alloying milieu43-45. APT results

also indicate pronounced enrichment of Al, Ni and Fe within the supra-nano precipitates

in the amorphous region (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 10f), supporting the

interpretation based on the TEM image in Fig. 3e. Notably, while amorphous-based

materials tend to crystallize over time46, subsequent in-situ heating TEM tests

(Supplementary Fig. 10g) and deformation microstructure analysis (Supplementary Fig.

9b) confirmed that these HMINPs-derived amorphous areas remain stable at 400 °C,

signifying their high thermal resistance.

As the tensile temperatures previously noted (300-400 °C) remained beneath the

melting threshold of the Al alloy, the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation (i.e.,

order-to-disorder transition) is triggered by solid-state amorphization. This transformation


<!-- Page 18 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

destabilizes the crystalline lattice and yields a disordered framework, which is markedly

distinct from the typical liquid-to-solid amorphous transformation observed during rapid

cooling43. Besides, the absence of amorphous zones within the as-printed sample (Fig.

1) and throughout in-situ heating procedures (Supplementary Fig. 5a) indicates that the

structural disorder leading to the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation is mainly

driven by extensive strain concentration during tensile deformation47. The activation

energy barrier for amorphization, signifying the energetic cost per unit volume necessary

for this transformation, often exhibits a temperature-dependent profile48. As plastic

deformation intensifies, the energy of the grain boundaries escalates, and elevated

temperatures empower atom activation, enabling them to deviate from their equilibrium

positions. Consequently, this enhances the activation energy and accelerates the

amorphization process. This elucidates the observation of amorphization solely during

tensile testing within the 300–400 °C range.

To deepen the understanding of the deformation mechanisms responsible for the

exceptional strength-ductility combination in Al alloy at 300–400 °C, it is essential to

distinguish the respective roles of dislocation-mediated plasticity and strain-induced

structural disorder. Three tensile samples (designated as S1, S2, and S3 hereafter) were

prepared from one [110] orientated grain (Fig. 4a), exhibiting remarkable tensile ductility

at 400 °C with an elongation exceeding 26%, roughly twice that observed in bulk samples.

In the in-situ TEM tensile experiments, deformation was primarily accommodated by

dislocation nucleation, motion, and pile-up, as well as their interactions with individual

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

precipitates and interfaces. Regions with relatively lower local precipitate density

facilitated direct visualization of these dislocation processes by reducing excessive strain

localization, enabling clearer identification of crack initiation pathways at elevated

temperatures. Specifically, crack initiation was observed in S1 at a strain of ~17.5%, with

cracks becoming evident in S2 and S3 at a strain of ~22.5%. A meticulous examination

of S1 revealed that the crack (pink arrow) originated along high-density nanoprecipitates

(Si + HMINPs, confirmed by TEM-EDS analysis) and subsequently propagated along

these precipitates (Fig. 4b). This interfacial cracking arose from substantial stress

concentrations caused by dislocation accumulation near these precipitates, as indicated

by white arrows. This failure mode aligns with the fracture mechanism at the interface

between the θ′ precipitates and the α-Al matrix, as reported in a previous study⁴⁹. In

contrast, crack initiation and propagation predominantly occurred within the Al matrix in

S2 and S3. In S2, crack initiation and growth transpired rapidly within the Al matrix (Fig.

4c). The crack propagation was accompanied by accumulation of dislocations in S3 (Fig.

4d). Further deformation revealed that cracks propagated along grain boundaries (Fig.

4e), known as weak points during high-temperature deformation. Notably, no fracture or

significant coarsening of HMINPs was observed during these high-temperature in-situ

TEM tensile tests, suggesting their exceptional thermal stability and ductility in

accommodating plastic deformation. However, no crystalline-to-amorphous transition

occurred during the TEM tensile tests at 400 °C. Owing to the presence of free surfaces

and reduced triaxial constraint in thin TEM samples, the defect energy density required


<!-- Page 20 -->

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

to trigger crystalline-to-amorphous transformation could not be sufficiently accumulated,

and no amorphization was therefore observed during in-situ tensile loading at 400 °C.

The deformation mechanism for these samples is consistent with that of conventional Al

alloys, where dislocation accumulation drives cracking and fracturing rather than

amorphization.

We finally investigated the bulk alloys deformed at 300–400 °C (within a strain range of

5%~9%) experienced sustained strain accumulation under higher constraint, leading to

reproducible solid-state amorphization of a portion of the HMINPs, as evidenced by TEM

and APT analyses (Supplementary Fig. 11). These amorphous phases underwent

substantial deformation during the final stage of tensile. By scrutinizing the microstructural

attributes of both submicron and bulk samples after deformation, we can succinctly

rationalize the high-temperature tensile deformation process of bulk Al alloys as follows:

as deformation energy accumulates and the density of defects (dislocations) increases

during tensile stress, elastic deformation transitions into the formation and motion of

dislocations. Ultimately, in the realm of high strain (and/or high strain rates) conditions, a

partial solid-state amorphization of ductile HMINPs emerges, giving rise to unique nano-

dual-phase glass-crystal structures that help harmonize deformation until failure45,48.

The amorphization process serves as a potent mechanism for alleviating substantial

deviatoric stresses that accumulate at the junctions of defects or transformation packets

44,45. The formation of an amorphous region induced by deformation provides an auxiliary


<!-- Page 23 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

pathway for energy dissipation and halts crack propagation during tensile tests, thereby

offering an effective toughening mechanism to maintain exceptional mechanical

properties45,47,48. The absence of crystal defects and dislocation glide pathways, which

are prevalent in crystalline materials, renders the amorphous phase resilient to both

tensile and creep deformation50,51. This attribute has been explored in

crystalline/amorphous nanolaminates52, magnetron sputtered supra-nano-dual-phase

glass-crystal Mg50 and Al53 alloys, all of which demonstrate synergetic ultrahigh strength

and resistance to crack initiation. Furthermore, the continuous generation-movement-

annihilation of dislocations between the amorphous phase and grains (e.g., Al matrix and

supra-nano γ’ phase in the present Al alloy) and the flow behavior of nano-sized

amorphous can further increase plasticity, as evidenced in our previous nanostructured

Al alloys53. Consequently, the present nano-dual-phase glass-crystal structure induced

by the solid-state amorphization introduces an extrinsic toughening mechanism during

tensile deformation at high temperatures (300-400 °C)44,50, aligning with the prolonged

elongation observed after peak strength (within a strain below 5%) in the tensile curves.

Although the detailed mechanisms behind this process are not yet fully understood, future

investigations utilizing molecular dynamics simulations could offer valuable insights into

the formation of both the amorphous phase and the supra-nano-sized particles within

it44,54.

In summary, we developed a facile and economically viable strategy to additively

manufacture strong yet ductile heat-resistant Al alloys, leveraging the common impurity

elements (Si, Fe, Ni, and Mn) in recyclable Al alloys. By embedding HMINPs at the

solidified cell boundaries, the resultant as-printed alloy boasts thermally stable cellular

structures with a remarkable high-volume fraction (~14 vol%). These unique structures

confer exceptional mechanical properties across a broad temperature range of 25-400 °C.

Notably, the as-printed alloy, without any supplementary treatment, exhibits a harmonious

blend of high tensile strength and ductility at ambient temperature, while also

demonstrating exceptional tensile and creep resistance at elevated temperatures.

Intriguingly, the solid-state amorphization of a portion of HMINPs during straining at 300-

400 °C emerges as an alternative toughening mechanism, ensuring the sustained

exceptional mechanical performance. Furthermore, the commercialization of this Al alloy

underscores its capacity to offer an excellent combination of affordable, lightweight

components with intricate geometric shapes for diverse applications. This work opens up

a new avenue for developing advanced materials with exceptional properties, enabling

transformative applications across multiple industries.

## Methods

Powder preparation

The raw powders for PBF-LB were prepared through the supersonic gas atomization

(GA) process, using a 50 kg cast ingot. The chemical composition of the raw powders (Al-

7.44Si-2.34Fe-1.79Mn-1.12Ni, wt %) and as-printed samples (Al-7.67Si-2.48Fe-1.83Mn-

1.27Ni, wt %) was determined using inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission


<!-- Page 25 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

spectroscopy. The content of Si and alloying elements (Fe, Mn, Ni) increased slightly after

printing, which is caused by the preferential evaporation of Al due to its relatively low

melting points55. The shape of the powders is highly spherical, with a few tiny satellites

on the surface, which is a common inherent defect during GA process56. The particle size

distribution of the powders was determined using the Malvern Mastersizer 3000, which

indicated D10, D50, and D90 values of 22.5 μm, 40.2 μm, and 56.6 μm, respectively. Laser

reflectivity of the raw powders was measured using diffuse reflectance spectroscopy on

a UV–visible–near-infrared SolidSpec-3700 spectrophotometer with a spectral resolution

of 1 nm. The laser reflectivity of the powders at a laser wavelength of 1070 nm was 33.7

± 0.1%, which was lower than that of other Al powders such as AlSi10Mg, 7075 Al, and

7075 Al alloys55, facilitating the enhancement of the efficiency of the MPs and saving

energy.

Laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing

The PBF-LB process of Al alloys was conducted on a commercial SLM Solutions 280

system under an argon atmosphere, with the oxygen level well controlled below 0.1 vol%.

The printing process was optimized with the following parameters: a laser power of 370

W, a scan speed of 1300 mm/s, a hatch spacing of 0.18 mm, a layer thickness of 0.03

mm, and a platform temperature of 25 °C (without preheating). A standard alternating x/y

raster scan pattern with a 67° angle between adjacent layers was employed as the

scanning strategy. The 10 × 10 × 10 mm3 cubic samples were prepared for densification


<!-- Page 26 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

and microstructural characterization, and cylinder samples with a length of 76 mm and a

diameter of 17 mm were printed for tensile testing.

Densification behavior

The internal defects of the as-printed samples was examined using a GE Phoenix

micro-focus CT (micro-CT) system operated at 190 kV and 20 μA. A small cubic specimen

(~3 × 3 × 3 mm³) was extracted from the center of the larger as-printed cubes using

electro-discharge machining for high-resolution imaging. During data acquisition, the

sample was rotated from 0° to 360° with a step size of 0.2°, and an exposure time of 500

ms per projection was used with a spatial resolution of 2024 × 2024 pixels, achieving a

voxel size of approximately 3.5 μm. The raw data were reconstructed into a 3D data field

using VGSTUDIO Max 3.2 software to reveal internal defect characteristics and quantify

the overall relative density. Although the use of a smaller sample is necessary for high-

resolution imaging, it may not fully reflect the distribution of extremely large or rare defects.

However, considering the high relative density (>99.9%) and process stability, the

measured volume provides a reliable assessment of the bulk material.

Microstructural characterizations

MPs in the Al alloy were observed using a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 optical microscope

(OM). For SEM, the as-printed samples were prepared using standard metallographic

procedures without chemical etching. TEM specimens were prepared by using twin-jet


<!-- Page 27 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

electropolishing on a Struers TenuPol-5 system, followed by ion milling with a Gatan PIPS

695. Microstructural and chemical composition analyses were conducted using an FEI

Quanta 450 SEM, a Talos TEM, and an FEI Titan Themis G2 TEM, each equipped with

EDS. In-situ heating experiments were performed in a spherical-aberration-corrected

Titan G2 environmental TEM, where samples were heated from room temperature to

target temperatures and held for 5 min to monitor microstructural evolution and thermal

stability. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) was performed on an FEI Scios

DualBeam FIB/SEM equipped with an EDAX Hikari high-speed detector. Data collection

was carried out at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 0.3 μm. For pattern

collection, a 4×4 binning mode was utilized, providing a good balance between spatial

resolution and acquisition speed. The indexing was based on the Hough transform

method. Data processing and orientation reconstruction were performed using TSL OIM

Analysis 8 software. To ensure data integrity, a Confidence Index (CI) cutoff of 0.1 was

applied. Following the cutoff, a standard Grain Dilation cleanup procedure (minimum grain

size of 5 pixels and a grain tolerance angle of 5°) was employed to remove minor indexing

artifacts. All reported data meet these quality thresholds, ensuring the reliability of the

orientation measurements.

The volume fraction of the multicomponent intermetallic nanophase was remeasured

using image analysis of the area fractions by employing a commercial software package

ImageJ (original ImageJ57), Over one hundred particles were included to determine an

average value. Phase identification was performed via XRD (Rigaku SmartLab instrument)

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

with Cu-Kα radiation at a scan speed of 2°/min. DSC experiments were performed on a

NETZSCH 404 F3 Pegasus system under an argon flow of 50 mL/min. As-printed

samples (~20 mg) were heated from 25 °C to 900 °C at 10 °C/min, held for 10 min, and

cooled to 25 °C at the same rate. Needle-shaped samples for 3D APT (CAMEACA LEAP

5000X HR) were prepared using the lift-out method and annular milling in an FEI Scios

Dual-Beam system in the APT unit. The samples were analyzed in laser mode with a

specimen temperature of 60 K, a laser energy of 30 pJ, a pulse rate of 200 kHz, and a

detection rate of 0.5%.

Tensile and creep tests

Tensile tests were conducted on both the transverse and longitudinal sections of the

as-printed samples. Round tensile specimens with a gauge length of 25 mm and a

diameter of 6.25 mm were machined from the printed cylinders using electro-discharge

machining (EDM). Tensile testing was performed on an MTS E45.105 machine in

accordance with ASTM E8 (room temperature, 25°C) and ASTM E21 standards (elevated

temperatures: 100 °C, 200 °C, 300 °C, and 400 °C). An initial strain rate of 0.005 min−1

was applied, and the rate was subsequently increased to 0.05 min−1 at 0.8% strain for the

elevated temperature tests to reduce the total test time, following the E21 protocol. Three

repeats were tested for each condition, and yield strength was determined by the 0.2%

offset method.

Tensile creep tests were carried out on the longitudinal sections of the as-printed


<!-- Page 29 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

samples. Standard creep specimens (GB/T 2039–2012) with a gauge length of 25 mm

and a diameter of 5 mm were extracted via EDM. Prior to testing, the samples were

heated from ambient temperature to 400 °C at 15 °C/min and held for 1 hour. Tensile

creep experiments were then performed at stresses of 25 MPa, 30 MPa, 32 MPa, and 40

MPa using an electronic high-temperature creep testing machine RDL10058.

Statistics & reproducibility

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. All data were included in

the analyses, and no data points were excluded. Sample sizes for mechanical and

microstructural tests were chosen based on standard practice in materials science to

ensure reliable measurements. Each test (e.g., laser reflectivity of the raw powders and

tensile tests at different temperatures) was repeated 3 times to confirm reproducibility.

Editor’s Summary This study highlights a strategy to additively manufacture lightweight, strong, and ductile heat-resistant aluminum alloys. The partial solid-state amorphization of the nanoprecipitates during high-temperature tension offers an additional toughening mechanism.
